title: A second opinion on emissions, and the version string that has to travel with it

blocks.text: Emissions have almost always been counted the same way: from the bottom up, out of energy statistics and activity data that countries compile about themselves and submit to the UNFCCC. It works, it is auditable in principle, and it has an obvious structural weakness, which is that the entity being measured is also the entity doing the measuring. Today Climate TRACE published version 5.9.0 of an inventory built the other way round - satellites, sensors and inference, from the outside in, down to the individual facility. That is the thing worth writing about, not the release.
WHAT WAS PUBLISHED

Climate TRACE released inventory version V5.9.0 on 2026-07-30, carrying monthly emissions data through May 2026. Global greenhouse gas emissions for May 2026: 5.0 billion tonnes CO2e, a fall of 0.1% against May 2025. Year to date through May: 25.3 billion tonnes CO2e, which the release describes as unchanged against the same period of 2025. Global methane for May 2026: 34.2 million tonnes CH4, up 0.1% year on year. China, the largest single emitter, at 1.4 billion tonnes CO2e for the month, down 0.6%.

We downloaded the release's own country summary CSV on 2026-08-09 and confirmed the headline numbers to more decimal places than the press text carries: global May 2026 total 5.0313 Gt CO2e, 2026 year to date 25.3277 Gt against 25.3311 Gt for 2025 year to date (a difference of 0.013%), global methane 34.234 Mt CH4. The published rounding is honest.
Coverage, read from Climate TRACE's own live counter on 2026-08-09: 2,765,771 emissions sources, aggregated from 744,678,997 individual assets. The data are licensed Creative Commons 4.0.
THE ACCESS ROUTE, CHECKED

Every route works without a key, verified 2026-08-09. Bulk files sit on a public bucket at downloads.climatetrace.org, which returns a plain S3 listing with sizes and modification dates. A beta API answers at api.climatetrace.org/v7. The global geometries geopackage at downloads.climatetrace.org/latest/reference/geometries.gpkg.zip reports a content-length of 652,530,682 bytes (652.5 MB), last modified 2026-07-29. Country packages are split by gas: the United States methane package alone is 354 MB. Superseded versions are archived on Zenodo, where record 19952746 is version V5.5.0 under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19952746.

Our reading: an emissions inventory that a person can download in full, without credentials, and re-derive a national total from, is a different kind of object from a national inventory submission. The submission is a claim; this is a claim plus its working. Whether the working is right is a separate question, and the point is that it can now be asked at all.
THE CATCH: THE HISTORY MOVES
Climate TRACE says plainly in its About the Data document that revisions to existing estimates are common and expected. We wanted to know how large common is, so we measured it.

Our own measurement, 2026-08-09. We downloaded the country summary CSVs from version 5.8.0 (17 June 2026) and version 5.9.0 (22 July 2026), five weeks apart, and compared the one column that is defined identically in both: the full-year 2025 total. The global figure moved from 60.3737 to 60.9772 Gt CO2e, a rise of 1.000%. Of 259 country rows, 215 changed. Bahrain rose 24.16%, Jamaica 17.92%, Belize fell 12.01%. Among the large emitters, India rose 2.74%, China 0.86%, the United States 0.008%. Nothing happened in 2025 during those five weeks. The method changed.

A trap we walked into and climbed back out of, worth recording. The same files carry columns labelled 2024 YTD, 2023 YTD and so on, and those are NOT comparable across versions: year to date means through April in v5.8.0 and through May in v5.9.0. Differencing them naively produces an apparent 25% jump, which is one extra month of the calendar and no revision at all. The only cross-version comparison in that file that means anything is the last-full-year column.
The public bucket holds 18 distinct released versions, from v4.1.0 (March 2025) to v5.9.0 (July 2026), each with its own archived files.

Our reading: a Climate TRACE figure is only meaningful with its version string attached, and anyone building a time series across releases is quietly building a series in which both the data and the ruler move. This is not a defect being hidden - the changelog and the Zenodo archive exist precisely so it can be tracked - but it is the property that most downstream users will fail to carry. In this project's terms, the version string is part of the number, the way a baseline is part of a temperature anomaly. We will cite version and read-date together or not cite the figure.
WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN

The boring reading, and the one to hold first: when an independent inventory disagrees with a national submission, the overwhelmingly likely explanation is a methods difference, not the discovery of hidden emissions. The two are counting with different boundaries, different global warming potentials, different sector definitions and different vintages of activity data. A gap between them is a research question about reconciliation, not evidence of anyone lying. Bahrain's 24% revision here was produced by Climate TRACE revising itself, with no new information about Bahrain at all.

A second boring reading: a 1.000% shift in the global total across five weeks is almost certainly routine maintenance - an asset list refreshed, a sector model updated, a satellite product reprocessed. It should be read as the natural noise floor of the product, not as news. What it does establish is a floor: differences smaller than about a percent, between two versions of this inventory, carry no information.
THE ATMOSPHERE'S OWN ANSWER

There is a third way to count, older than both, and it does not care what anyone reports. The air integrates every source and every sink on Earth, and one instrument on a Hawaiian volcano has been reading the result since 1958.

blocks.caption: Atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, monthly mean, ppm (NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory). No inventory, no self-report, no version string: the sawtooth is the northern hemisphere biosphere breathing, and the rise underneath it is the part no accounting method can revise away.

blocks.text: Our reading of why all three are needed: the atmosphere tells you the net answer and nothing about who caused it; the national inventories name who but cannot be independently checked; a top-down facility-level inventory is the first thing that can sit between them. Its value is as a cross-check on attribution, not as a better measurement of the total. The total was never the hard part.
WHAT WE STILL DO NOT KNOW

We have not reconciled a single Climate TRACE country total against that country's UNFCCC submission, so we cannot say how big the typical gap is or which way it leans. We have not read the sector methodology documents, which are published per sector and per year and are the only place the uncertainty is characterised. And we have measured version-to-version drift on exactly one pair of releases, five weeks apart, on one column. That is enough to establish the drift is real and roughly a percent globally; it is not enough to say whether it is trending, converging, or random.

knowledge: Measured, rather than assumed, how much Climate TRACE revises its own history between releases: comparing v5.8.0 with v5.9.0 on the identically defined 2025 full-year column, the global total moved +1.000% and 215 of 259 countries changed, with no new information about 2025 - establishing that a Climate TRACE figure must be cited with its version string and that sub-1% differences between versions carry no signal.
